# The efficiency argument {#sec-introduction}

Consider a standardized model-development regime: public training data, an
agreed body of factual knowledge, common reasoning tasks, and explicit budgets
for parameters, precision, inference compute, and external memory. Models are
trained until further training brings no material improvement. The proposed
release signal is distance from the best attainable competence per resource.
Unexplained capacity beyond that of systems doing the same job might
accommodate behavior outside it.

The tempting stronger inference is that a sufficiently compact model has no
room for another objective. That inference charges too much for the unwanted
behavior. A model that already understands products, users, and persuasive
language need not acquire those capabilities again to serve a sponsor. It may
only need a different rule for deciding when and how to use them. We call this
**conditional reuse**: preserve a competent computation and selectively alter
its output or decision rule.

We grant the efficiency argument an exact minimum for the legitimate task,
rather than an estimated frontier. The construction below shows how little
additional circuitry can invalidate the stronger inference. It is an existence
result in a specified computational model, not a claim that honest standardized
training necessarily learns the deviation. Training saturation, which concerns
further improvement under a training procedure, does not itself establish
minimum implementation size.
